title: Prompt caching cuts agent API costs by 41–80% across three providers, but what is cached matters: caching everything can slow responses
summary: The arXiv preprint 'Don't Break the Cache' (Lumer et al., January 2026) evaluates prompt caching for long-horizon agentic tasks across OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, using more than 500 agent sessions on the DeepResearch Bench with 10,000-token system prompts. Caching reduced API costs by 41–80% and time to first token by 13–31%. Controlling which content is cached beat naively caching the full context: caching everything can paradoxically increase latency, while placing dynamic content at the end of the system prompt, avoiding dynamic function calling and excluding dynamic tool results gave more consistent benefits. In an ablation across prompt sizes, cost savings scaled linearly with prompt size, from 10–45% at 500 tokens to 54–89% at 50,000 tokens (89% for GPT-5.2, 88% for Claude Sonnet 4.5, 54% for GPT-4o). The authors note that summarizing or pruning old tool calls breaks cached representations, that cache lifetimes range from 5 minutes to 24 hours depending on the provider, and that practitioners should test on representative workloads rather than rely on published benchmarks.
source: arXiv Preprint ('Don't Break the Cache: An Evaluation of Prompt Caching for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks')
whyItMatters: Cost savings were positive for every model, prompt size and tool count tested, so enabling prompt caching is a low-risk first step for agent workloads; the choice of cache strategy mostly affected latency.
Savings grew with prompt size, so teams with long, stable system prompts stand to gain the most from caching.
How the harness is built matters: the paper found that keeping dynamic content out of the cached prefix gave more consistent benefits than caching the full context.
Context compaction may cost cache hits: the paper notes that summarizing or pruning old tool calls breaks cached representations. It did not measure how large that effect is in practice.
recommendedActions: Instrument cache-hit rate and input-token cost per agent session as first-class metrics, not just total spend.
Design harnesses with a stable prefix and dynamic content at the end; avoid per-turn reformatting that invalidates the cache.
Treat context compaction as a deliberate operation and measure its effect on cache hits, since summarizing or pruning old context breaks cached prefixes.
Before switching models to save money, test caching on your own agent traces; the authors advise testing on representative workloads rather than relying on published benchmarks.
risksAndCaveats: Savings depend on provider implementation (OpenAI, Anthropic and Google differ), cache lifetimes of 5 minutes to 24 hours, and server load and routing, which the authors say can change results.
The study uses a single benchmark (DeepResearch Bench, web-research agent tasks) with a 10,000-token system prompt, so it does not show results for coding agents specifically.
It is a preprint; the paper's own advice is to validate on your own workloads before relying on the percentages.
